title: The Magical Compliments Board
markdown:
Willow Creek Elementary had a brand new notice board, painted a cheerful blue, standing proudly by the main entrance. Its official title: the Compliments Board. Entrusted with its upkeep was Lily, niece of Mr Fitzwilliam, the school’s ever-busy janitor. Lily herself was quiet, like the rustle of leaves on a still autumn day. But her eyes missed nothing. The tiniest fidgets. The subtlest smiles. The way a teacher’s shoulders would straighten just a bit. When she put those details into words, they shone.

Wren, a wolf cub with fur the colour of dawn mist, ears always twitching, was a gentle soul, happier tracing patterns in fallen leaves than tumbling about. Beside him was Sumi, a stoat so quick and bright she was like a flash of sunlight on a river stone. Loyalty clung to her whiskers. Guiding them, Aunt Mara, a wise old owl, spectacles often sliding down her beak as she pondered.

Wren padded up, tail giving a shy swish. “What’s this, Sumi?” Soft as moss.

Sumi darted beside him. “Looks like a board for saying nice things. Finally, someone’s going to notice my superior acorn-finding skills!” Whiskers twitched with genuine interest anyway.

Wren peered closer. A card sat neatly pinned. He read aloud. “To Mr Henderson, our geography teacher: Your lessons make the world feel so close, it’s like I can smell the desert sand and feel the ocean spray. Thank you for the journeys.”

Sumi blinked. “Smell the desert sand? Did he hide a little sandbox behind the board?”

Wren chuckled, a low rumble, and moved his paw to the next card. “To Mrs Gable, the art teacher: Your encouragement yesterday was like a warm sunbeam on a shy little sprout. It helped me bloom.”

“Bloom?” Sumi hopped. “Are compliments supposed to make you grow taller? I could use a few extra inches for the juiciest berries.”

Aunt Mara glided down from a high branch, wings a soft swish like turning pages. Landed on a nearby bench, wise eyes twinkling. “Ah, the compliments. Lily’s work, I imagine. She has a most remarkable way of seeing what others overlook.”

“Seeing is one thing,” Wren said, brow furrowed. “But these are quite grand. Like describing a whole country with just a few words.”

And they were. For the librarian, always balancing a mountain of books: Your ability to find the perfect book in a sea of spines is like a skilled cartographer navigating uncharted waters. For the quiet man who tended the school’s unruly garden: The way you coax the shyest seedlings to unfurl is truly a quiet miracle. The garden breathes because of you.

Soon a delightful buzz filled Willow Creek. Not the usual playground chatter. A genuine warm hum of appreciation. Teachers stood a little straighter. Students, inspired, began to offer their own kind words, hesitant at first, then with growing confidence. The air seemed to shimmer with an extra layer of kindness.

The compliments were so vivid they started to… well, to go to people’s heads, as if metaphors had put on boots. Mr Henderson, after reading about smelling desert sand, found himself sniffing the air during lessons, convinced he caught cinnamon from his talk about the spice trade. Mrs Gable’s class, inspired by painting with the colours of joy, produced a canvas so blindingly bright it looked more like a sun exploding than a happy scene. The librarian, burdened by uncharted waters, started recommending books on shipbuilding even to children asking for fairy tales.

The real diplomatic crisis descended upon the head teacher, Ms Periwinkle, who managed her school with the quiet efficiency of a well-oiled machine. Kind, but rather to-the-point. The compliment for her read: Dear Ms Periwinkle, your leadership is a sturdy oak, its branches sheltering us all from any storm, its roots deep in wisdom and care.

She usually walked with firm footing. But the oak. She looked at her own rather slender frame, then at the magnificent oak outside her office window. The weight of being a sheltering tree felt immense. She found herself sighing more, her brisk stride becoming a thoughtful, almost hesitant amble.

The staff room, normally tea and gentle grumbles about misplaced pencils, became a maze of exaggerated praise. “Can you believe it, Lily?” Henderson exclaimed, nearly knocking over a potted plant. “I’m practically an explorer charting continents every time I write on the board. And I swear I can still smell the salt from Portugal.”

Periwinkle sat hunched. The compliment felt like a heavy cloak. She tried to stand taller, to feel imagined roots, but her knees felt wobbly, like a young sapling in a strong wind. “I feel more like a twig than a tree,” she confessed to a bewildered colleague. “This is all very… overwhelming.”

Gentle chaos escalated. The music teacher, praised for conducting the melodies of happiness, had the choir belting cheerful tunes until the windows rattled. The sports coach, lauded for igniting the spirit of champions, had everyone attempting cartwheels at break, a comical flurry of tumbles rather than triumphs.

Finally Periwinkle, with a sigh that could have wilted a field of daisies, declared a special assembly. Wren, Sumi, and Mara found prime seats in the front row. Periwinkle stood at the podium, a teetering stack of extraordinary compliment cards in her hand.

“My dear students and colleagues, we find ourselves awash in magnificent, powerful, and perhaps slightly overwhelming praise. I am deeply touched. I also fear we may be losing sight of the simple quiet goodness that makes Willow Creek special. We risk being adrift in fancy words.”

A small, usually silent figure rose. Lily walked with determined if small steps to the front. Hands clasped. Small frame even smaller against the stage.

“Ms Periwinkle? It was me. I wrote them.”

Surprised murmurs. Wren’s ears shot up. Sumi’s tail froze mid-flick.

“I watch,” Lily continued, a faint blush, gaze steady. “I see Mr Henderson, how his eyes light up when he talks about faraway places, how he points to the map with such passion it feels like he’s there. And Mrs Gable, the way she gently guides a child’s brush, coaxing their own colours, like the sun helping the smallest seed. And you,” she looked at the head teacher, “you always listen, always help, even when things are difficult. You’re like a strong, safe tree that everyone can lean on.”

She had not invented the praise. She had observed the genuine kindness, the quiet dedication, the sparks of passion. She used metaphors because they felt fitting, grand, for the wonderful things she witnessed.

“I didn’t mean to make it confusing, or to make you feel too much pressure. I just wanted everyone to know they were appreciated.”

Periwinkle looked at Lily, then at the pile of compliments, then back at the small girl. A slow genuine smile, warm and bright. She stepped down and knelt. “Lily. You haven’t caused a crisis. You’ve shown us something more valuable. Thoughtful observation. You’ve helped us see the good in each other, not just feel it.”

The Compliments Board did not vanish. It was transformed. Lily continued her beautifully worded observations, but now everyone was encouraged to add their own. Simpler notes, perhaps — a shared smile, a helpful gesture — no less sincere. Henderson’s geography lessons still took them on journeys, but he no longer expected sand in his tweed. Gable’s class still burst with colour, the joyful colour of making. And Periwinkle, still steady, no longer felt the overwhelming weight of a mighty oak, only the quiet enduring strength of the wise tree she truly was.

Wren nudged Sumi, heart swelling. “Sometimes the most exciting adventures are the ones where we learn to look a little closer.”

Sumi nodded, already buzzing. Perhaps their next escapade would involve a compliment for a particularly tricky puzzle, or a very grumpy badger. Aunt Mara, from a high branch, adjusted her spectacles, a soft hoot of contentment. The warm glow of genuine appreciation remained, far more precious than any hidden treasure. The greatest wonders, if you looked closely, were often the simplest of things.
characters: Wren (a wolf cub), Sumi (a stoat), Mara (an owl)
